title: Letters to a Young Poet (Letter One)
author: Rainer Maria Rilke
citation: Rilke, Rainer Maria. Letters to a Young Poet. Translated by M.D. Herter Norton, W.W. Norton & Company, 1993, pp. 5–12.

sections.heading: Letter One: Paris, February 17, 1903

epigraph.quote: Go into yourself. Search for the reason that bids you write; find out whether its roots are spread out in the deepest depths of your heart.

paragraphs: Your letter only reached me a few days ago. I want to thank you for the great and kind confidence it showed. There is little more that I can do, I cannot discuss the nature of your verses; for any attempt at criticism is far from me. Nothing touches a work of art so little as words of criticism: they always result in more or less fortunate misunderstandings. Things are not all so comprehensible and expressible as one would usually have us believe; most events are inexpressible, take place in an arena which no word has ever entered, and more inexpressible than all else are works of art, mysterious existences, the life of which, while our own passes away, endures.

Having said this before everything, let me only tell you further that your verses have no peculiar character of their own, though they do have silent and hidden beginnings of something personal. I feel this most distinctly in the last poem, 'My Soul.' There, something of your own is trying to get into word and tune. And in the lovely poem 'To Leopardi' there arises, perhaps, a kind of kinship with that great, solitary man. Still, the poems are not yet anything in themselves, not yet independent, even the last one and the one to Leopardi. Your kind letter, which accompanied them, did not fail to make clear to me various defects that I sensed in reading your verses, though I could not name them specifically.

You ask whether your verses are any good. You ask me. You have asked others before this. You send them to magazines. You compare them with other poems, and you are upset when certain editors reject your work. Now (since you have allowed me to give you advice) I beg you to stop doing that sort of thing. You are looking outward, and that above all you should not do now. Nobody can advise and help you, nobody. There is only one way: Go into yourself. Search for the reason that bids you write; find out whether its roots are spread out in the deepest depths of your heart; confess to yourself whether you would have to die if you were forbidden to write. This most of all: ask yourself in the most silent hour of your night: must I write? Delve into yourself for a deep answer. And if this should be affirmative, if you may meet this solemn question with a strong and simple 'I must,' then build your life according to this necessity; your life even into its most indifferent and slightest hour must be a sign of this impulse and a testimony to it.

Then come close to nature. Then try, as if no one had ever tried before, to say what you see and feel and love and lose. Do not write love poems; avoid at first those forms that are too familiar and commonplace: they are the most difficult, for it takes a great, fully matured power to give something of your own where good and even brilliant traditions exist in plenty. Therefore turn from these general themes to those which your own everyday life affords; describe your sorrows and desires, the passing thoughts and the belief in some sort of beauty—describe all these with loving, quiet, humble sincerity, and use, to express yourself, the things in your environment, the images from your dreams, and the objects of your memory.

If your daily life seems poor, do not blame it; blame yourself that you are not poet enough to call forth its riches; for the Creator, there is no poverty and no poor, indifferent place. And even if you found yourself in some prison, whose walls let through none of the sounds of the world—would you not still have your childhood, that jewel beyond all price, that treasure house of memories? Turn your attention thither. Try to raise up the sunken feelings of that vast past; your personality will grow stronger, your solitude will expand and will become a quiet room where the noise of other people goes by in the distance.

And if from this turning inward, from this sinking into your own world, verses come, you will not think of asking anyone whether they are good verses. Nor will you attempt to interest magazines in these works: for you will see in them your beloved natural possession, a piece and a voice of your life. A work of art is good if it has arisen out of necessity. In this nature of its origin lies its judgment: there is no other. Therefore, my dear Sir, I could give you no advice but this: to go into yourself and explore the depths where your life wells forth; at its source you will find the answer to the question whether you must write.

Accept it, just as it sounds, without inquiring into it. Perhaps it will turn out that you are called to be an artist. Then take that destiny upon yourself, and bear it, its burden and its greatness, without ever asking what recompense might come from outside. For the creator must be a world for himself and find everything in himself and in nature to which he has attached himself.

Perhaps, too, after this descent into yourself and into your solitude you will have to give up becoming a poet (it is enough, as I have said, to feel that one could live without writing: then one must not do it at all). But even then, this inward searching that I ask of you will not have been in vain. Your life will in any case find its own ways from there, and that they may be good, rich, and wide I wish you more than I can say.

What more shall I say to you? Everything seems to me to have its right emphasis; and I want to wish you further that you may quietly and seriously continue your development; you could not disturb it more sharply than by looking outward and expecting from the outside answers to questions that only your most inward feeling in your most quiet hour can perhaps answer.

It was a joy to me to find in your letter the name of Professor Horacek; I preserve for that lovable scholar a great veneration and a gratefulness that lasts through the years. Will you please tell him how I feel; it is very good of him still to think of me, and I know how to appreciate it.

The verses that you kindly entrusted to me I am returning to you at the same time. And I thank you once more for the greatness and affection of your trust, of which I have tried to make myself a little more worthy than, as a stranger, I really am, through this sincere answer, written to the best of my knowledge and belief.

Yours faithfully and with great sympathy,
RAINER MARIA RILKE
